video.title: The Amazon Program Almost Nobody Is Actually Doing (Full-Time)

summary: Nate describes earning commissions by filming short product review videos and placing them on Amazon product pages; the videos can earn without an outside audience. His approach favors making many simple videos of products already available over extensive research and editing, while using product access, brand campaigns, and cross-posting to expand the business. He also explains ways to find products, including filming at neighbors’ homes and requesting brand samples, and discusses reselling products and coaching. The central takeaway is to start publishing, learn through practice, and treat the income and Amazon placement as variable rather than guaranteed.

ideas.name: Amazon on-site influencer product videos
ideas.one_liner: Film product review videos, tag the matching Amazon listing, and earn commissions when shoppers buy.
ideas.business_model: Commission on attributed product sales, with additional commissions possible through Creator Connections campaigns.
ideas.customer: Amazon shoppers considering a product on its listing page.
ideas.problem: Shoppers want a firsthand look at a product and reassurance that it suits their needs before buying.
ideas.offer: Short product videos showing features, size, use, pros, cons, comparisons, or updates; videos are uploaded and tagged to the relevant Amazon product listing.

pricing.model: Commission per attributed sale; brand-funded Creator Connections commissions may supplement Amazon commissions.

price_points.label: Amazon commission example for a doorknob
Brand campaign example for an Apple Watch strap

pricing.notes: Rates depend on product and campaign. Nate says Amazon does not provide much performance data.

acquisition_channels.details: Upload and tag videos on Amazon listings. Amazon may surface them in upper or lower video carousels, where shoppers can watch while considering the product. Nate says this does not require outside marketing.

quote.text: I upload that, tag it as the product on Amazon. Somebody, no outside marketing. Amazon shows that on the product page.
quote.speaker: Host

acquisition_channels.details: Nate recommends trying an existing public social account to apply for the program. If rejected, he suggests creating a TikTok account in a niche, engaging with related posts, and posting questions or rage bait to generate comments. This is for program approval, not Amazon shopper acquisition.

quote.text: If you get a bunch of comments on TikTok, we've basically solved the equation.
quote.speaker: Nate

ideas.delivery: The creator finds a product, films it with a phone or camera, and uploads the video to Amazon with the product tagged. Videos range from quick surface-level reviews to longer demonstrations, comparisons, unboxings, and updates. Nate often appears on camera but says it is optional. Amazon displays videos and handles order attribution and commission payments; brands can separately pay campaign commissions. Filming and handling physical products remain human work.
unit_economics_claims: Nate says he can make $20,000 per month from the business.
Nate says he is satisfied with $1 per month per video and reports a beginner-to-mid-level average of about $1.50 to $2.50 per video per month.
Nate reports that a 12-minute shed video made a couple thousand dollars.
Nate says Amazon commissions can be around 1–2% for a doorknob, while Creator Connections campaigns may pay 10–50%.
tools: Amazon product listings and video carousels
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; Nate says beginners can start with products already in their homes.

acquisition.how: Amazon listings and carousels provide inbound shopper discovery, but creators cannot control placement and must make and upload the videos.

onboarding.how: Program application and approval require human judgment and may involve manually building engagement on a social account.

delivery.how: A person must access and film the physical product. Uploading or cross-posting can be tool-assisted, but the review itself is human work.

billing.how: Amazon and brand campaigns can track attributed sales and pay commissions automatically, with occasional human checks needed for reporting.

support.how: Amazon handles the customer transaction, but the transcript does not describe creator support processes; product questions or corrections may still need human attention.

uk_applicability.notes: The product-page video and commission model appears portable, but the transcript discusses the US marketplace. A UK founder would need to check UK program eligibility, product availability, campaign terms, and commission rates.

risks: Amazon placement is algorithmic, can change without notice, and is not guaranteed.
Videos and earnings can decay over time; Amazon provides limited data for diagnosing performance.
High volume can mean many videos earn nothing, while a smaller number may account for much of the income.
Rage bait may create engagement but can damage trust and reputation; claims about products should remain accurate.
The transcript says Amazon removed on-site related-sale credit in April, reducing the value of some negative reviews.
Do not film products inside stores such as Walmart or Target; Nate says this can get an account removed.
Unsolicited brand messages sent at scale could create UK PECR issues when recipients are individuals or sole traders; outreach should be limited to lawful recipients or consented channels.

ideas.name: Reselling free brand samples

ideas.business_model: Resale margin on products received free from brands; review commissions or brand payments may provide additional income.
ideas.customer: Marketplace buyers seeking the products being resold.
ideas.problem: Buyers want products available through resale listings; brands want creator coverage and sales.
ideas.offer: Request samples from brands, create content about them, and list the items on resale marketplaces.

pricing.model: Resale proceeds, potentially combined with review commissions or brand payments.
pricing.notes: No resale prices or sample payment amounts are specified.

acquisition_channels.details: Nate discusses requesting samples through Creator Connections and reselling products on Facebook Marketplace or eBay.
Nate says messages can be sent to brands requesting products, but does not explain a compliant process for UK outreach.

ideas.delivery: The creator requests and receives product samples, creates review videos, then lists and sells the products through resale marketplaces. Listing, packing, shipping, and handling inventory require human work.
unit_economics_claims: Nate says he believes anyone with enough time to list products can make $40,000 to $50,000 a year reselling free samples.
ideas.startup_cost: Products may be received free; other startup costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: Automated brand messaging is mentioned, but unsolicited electronic messages to individuals or sole traders can be unlawful in the UK; recipients and consent need checking.

onboarding.how: Campaign applications and sample requests may be submitted online, but eligibility and product selection need human review.

delivery.how: A person must receive, store, list, pack, and ship physical products.

billing.how: Marketplaces can process payments, but pricing, listing fees, and payout records need human oversight.

support.how: Returns, shipping questions, and buyer issues involve physical inventory and likely require human handling.

uk_applicability.notes: Online resale is portable to the UK, but platform rules, shipping, tax, and the availability of brand sample campaigns differ.

risks: Sample campaigns may attract many creators, reducing the chance that a product performs well.
Receiving and disposing of packaging takes time and can create waste-management problems at high volume.
Resale requires time to list and handle inventory; the claimed annual income is not supported with a detailed cost breakdown.
Automated cold messaging may breach UK PECR when sent to individuals or sole traders without consent.

tactics.name: Apply with an existing social account, then build engagement if rejected
steps: Try a public account you already have, such as Facebook, YouTube, Pinterest, or TikTok.
If rejected, choose a niche for a new TikTok account.
Follow a few niche accounts, like and comment on related posts, then post niche content consistently for about two weeks.
Use questions to invite comments; Nate also suggests rage bait, which may harm trust and should be used cautiously.

quote.text: If you've got a public Facebook page, you've got a big YouTube, you've got even a small YouTube.
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Start with products already at hand
steps: Walk through your home and identify products, household hardware, furniture, books, clothing, tools, and used items that match Amazon listings.
Film an item you already own instead of spending the same time researching whether it is a perfect opportunity.
Use a visual search tool to match an item to a listing before filming; Nate says not to film first and match later.

quote.text: I could spend that same five minutes simply making a video for this mouse and uploading it and doing zero research.
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Keep simple reviews quick and useful
steps: Use a phone or camera and talk through what the product is, what you like, what you dislike, and who it suits.
Show the item in use when practical; use a face-on-camera format when it helps, but film the product alone when that is clearer.
Skip editing out minor mistakes or the start button when the edit adds no useful information.
Use ChatGPT for talking points if a beginner needs help structuring a review.

quote.text: I just point my camera, I hold the product like with this mouse, I keep the mouse close to my face.
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Test length and format against the likely shopper
steps: Nate's current videos average two to three minutes; he previously aimed for roughly 45 to 85 seconds.
Test making a video 30% to 50% longer to increase watch time, while recognizing that Amazon's placement algorithm changes.
Use vertical video when shoppers are more likely to be on phones, such as for fashion or children's products; use horizontal for desktop-oriented products.
Try additional formats on the same product, such as an unboxing, an update, or a second orientation.

quote.text: So for me, that's been make my videos maybe 30 to 50% longer than I normally would, and that seemed to be working well for me.
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Make multiple useful angles for strong products
steps: For a product that merits more coverage, make separate videos for unboxing, setup, features, mistakes, comparison, and a later update.
Use measurements or real-life demonstrations when they answer a likely shopper question.
Keep the review honest, including problems with a product and who should avoid it.

quote.text: So you can kind of come at it from so many different angles. There's not like a one size fits all for these things.
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Use nearby households and real environments as product sources
steps: Ask neighbors or friends for permission to film products they already own.
Nate offered a $20 Starbucks gift card for an afternoon of access to a large Lego collection.
Offer to house-sit or return for another session if a household has more products than can be filmed in one visit.
Film products in their natural environment, such as a handwashing station at a market, but do not film products inside retail stores.

quote.text: I went to a couple of these houses. And I mean, I kid you not. These people have entire basements.
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Prioritize products with campaign commissions and manageable competition
steps: Scan possible products and check influencer counts and Creator Connections campaign information.
When time is limited, prioritize products with a strong campaign rate and fewer competing influencers.
Treat selection filters such as 500 monthly units, zero influencers, or a 20% campaign rate as examples to test, not guaranteed predictors.

quote.text: I need to sort of prioritize stuff. So I'll use that to do some visual scans.
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Ask brands for samples, but account for the work and competition
steps: Find relevant Creator Connections campaigns and send a clear request to the brand for a product to review.
Do not assume the campaign statement about samples means the brand will refuse; Nate says it may be boilerplate.
Track response rates and product handling time, and do not let free samples crowd out simpler products already available.
In the UK, screen the recipient type and ensure any electronic marketing outreach complies with PECR.

quote.text: So request anything you want, and about 10% are going to reach back to you and say, OK, great.
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Cross-post completed videos automatically
steps: Set up Chiching to download Amazon videos, add descriptions and titles, change thumbnails, add affiliate links, and upload them to YouTube.
Let the tool run in the background, then check that uploads and links are correct.
Treat YouTube as an incremental revenue stream unless you are intentionally producing content for YouTube viewers.

quote.text: So I let this run and it usually runs like 10 to 20 videos per day 'cause I have a lot of videos
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Try low-cost returns stock and resell products that do not perform
steps: Look for local return-bin or liquidation outlets and scan products before buying.
Compare product cost with the expected resale price, campaign terms, and marketplace fees.
List unwanted or reviewed products for resale through marketplaces; consider live selling only if enough inventory accumulates.

tactics.name: Build a second income stream as a safety net
steps: Nate says he is building a YouTube channel and coaching activity so he has some income if Amazon shuts down his account.
Keep secondary revenue sources as a baseline rather than assuming they will replace the main business.

quote.text: I've been doing some coaching with people down just helping to teach other people how to do this.
quote.speaker: Nate

warnings.warning: Do not overinvest in product research or production before publishing; Nate says beginners often get stuck in analysis paralysis.

quote.text: I just got into analysis paralysis where I felt like, "Okay, I need to do all these things,
quote.speaker: Nate

warnings.warning: Amazon carousel placement is partly random and the algorithm changes, so do not assume one video length or title tactic will always work.

quote.text: You can't put too much effort into trying to gain the system or whatever, but where I can put my effort in, I will try.
quote.speaker: Nate

warnings.warning: Nate says not to film products on retail shelves in stores such as Walmart or Target because Amazon may remove an account.

quote.text: That's gonna get you kicked off really, really fast. 'Cause that is not that product's next.
quote.speaker: Nate

warnings.warning: Free samples can create crowding, slower production, and packaging disposal work; a product that looks attractive in shared data may have many competing creators.

quote.text: If they're sending me a free sample, they're probably willing to send you a free sample and 10 other people for example.
quote.speaker: Nate

warnings.warning: Nate says on-site related-sale credit was removed in April, so negative reviews no longer earn related sales in the same way.

quote.text: But now that only works for off-site videos. If I made a YouTube video about that fish tank and people bought a different fish tank, then I would still get the different credit.
quote.speaker: Nate

warnings.warning: Do not assume every video will earn; Nate describes many videos earning nothing and a small number earning more.

quote.text: Plenty of your videos are gonna make $0 a month. A couple of them will make maybe $10 a month.
quote.speaker: Nate

warnings.warning: Automated brand outreach should be checked against UK marketing rules, especially for messages to individuals and sole traders.
Nate says not to expect a large income for doing no work; the business still requires filming, product handling, and continued effort.

quote.text: Yes, the program's not as easy as it used to be, but no one should expect to be making 10 grand a month for doing zero work.
quote.speaker: Host

lessons.lesson: Publish a simple first version instead of waiting for ideal research, equipment, titles, or editing; practice improves the process.

quote.text: Stop overthinking it. If it's the influencer program, just start making your videos.
quote.speaker: Nate

lessons.lesson: When products are already available to film, the opportunity cost of researching every item may exceed the cost of trying a quick video.

quote.text: In the other scenario, I have a more than zero percent chance of making some money.
quote.speaker: Nate

lessons.lesson: A high-volume approach spreads effort across many videos, but it also means accepting that many videos may earn nothing.

quote.text: And eventually, again, just like what you said, just by the law of large numbers, I will have products that are very, very good products.
quote.speaker: Nate

lessons.lesson: Use the product listing as context: shoppers are already considering a purchase, so a useful confirmation can matter more than a hard sell.

quote.text: I am there to just confirm with them. Yes, you're not crazy. This is a good purchase and it will fit your needs.
quote.speaker: Nate

lessons.lesson: Honest negative feedback can build trust and still help a shopper decide; explain the real drawback and any appropriate alternative use.

quote.text: finally, someone who's being honest with us, they're not just trying to like sell us and hype something up, they're being honest.
quote.speaker: Nate

lessons.lesson: Prefer incremental experiments over trying to solve an algorithm that changes and exposes only partial performance data.

quote.text: I don't think it will ever be a solved equation. It's something that you can kind of always tinker with and play with a little bit
quote.speaker: Nate

lessons.lesson: For physical product videos, show the item in a real setting when that setting helps shoppers understand how it works.

quote.text: They want you inside of stores. So don't go to like Target or Walmart and just start filming everything off the shelf.
quote.speaker: Nate

lessons.lesson: Treat free samples as a sourcing option, not automatically as the best growth strategy; competition and handling time can erase the appeal.

quote.text: So do I get free samples? Yeah, I've got a couple of free samples today. Is that like a huge part of my business? Not really.
quote.speaker: Nate

lessons.lesson: Build a second revenue stream to reduce reliance on one platform and create a financial safety net.

quote.text: I would like sort of a baseline like, okay, if everything hits the fan, I can still pay my mortgage.
quote.speaker: Nate

lessons.lesson: Longer-lived content can keep earning after the production work is done, but past earnings do not remove the need to keep creating if income is declining.

quote.text: Are you kidding me? That's incredible. And when you break down the times, like you said, you had 60 videos.
quote.speaker: Host

lessons.lesson: Do not count on extreme income forecasts without considering account risk, changing algorithms, decay, and the labor needed to keep producing.

quote.text: No one should expect to be making 10 grand a month for doing zero work. That's not how life works.
quote.speaker: Host

evidence_quality.rationale: Nate gives a first-hand account with concrete production methods, sourcing examples, and some specific performance figures. The figures are self-reported, some market-wide claims are estimates, and Amazon placement and attribution are described as changing or only partly observable.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Nate promotes the Amazon Influencer Hub, Hustle Buddies group, and coaching. The host also reads sponsor ads for Shopify, Monarch, Gusto, and Quo; those sponsor products were not treated as business ideas.
